name: Black Hole Threaded by a Cosmic String
description: A Schwarzschild black hole with a straight cosmic string through it. Off the axis it is Schwarzschild's vacuum, and around the whole axis, horizon included, a wedge is missing whose angle the string's tension sets, which lowers the horizon's area and the black hole's energy at a fixed mass.
convention: The Schwarzschild radius is $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, and $b = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$ for a string of mass per unit length $\mu$, so the deficit angle is $2\pi(1 - b) = 8\pi G\mu/c^2$. We keep factors of $c$ explicit.
history: Mukunda Aryal, Larry Ford, and Alexander Vilenkin wrote down in 1986 the metric of a Schwarzschild black hole with a straight cosmic string passing through it [aryal1986]. The space around a straight string of mass per unit length $\mu$ is flat, with a wedge of angle $8\pi G\mu/c^2$ missing from every plane the string crosses [vilenkin1981, gott1985]. Their metric is Schwarzschild's with $\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2$ multiplied by $(1 - 4G\mu/c^2)^2$, which puts a conical singularity along the whole axis, $\theta = 0$ and $\theta = \pi$, where the string lies [aryal1986, achucarro1995]. The tension is the same on both halves of the axis, so the black hole stays at rest [appels2017]. With the angle $(1 - 4G\mu/c^2)\phi$ in place of $\phi$ the line element is Schwarzschild's, and that angle runs over $2\pi - 8\pi G\mu/c^2$ [achucarro1995, appels2017].¶Aryal, Ford, and Vilenkin showed that the entropy of the black hole is still a quarter of the area of its horizon, $S = A/4$ in units with $G = \hbar = c = k_B = 1$ [aryal1986]. The horizon is a sphere of radius $r_s$ with the wedge missing, of area $A = 4\pi(1 - 4G\mu/c^2)r_s^2$ [appels2017]. They noted that the Schwarzschild mass parameter $M$, the gravitational mass of the system, no longer equals its energy [aryal1986]. Erik Martinez and James York studied the same spacetime with the Euclidean action in 1990 and concluded that the merging of a black hole and a string is not thermodynamically forbidden [martinez1990]. Ana Achúcarro, Ruth Gregory, and Konrad Kuijken found in 1995 that the internal energy of the black hole is $(1 - 4G\mu/c^2)Mc^2$, the energy of a spherical shell of matter that falls in from infinity around the string to form it [achucarro1995]. Its temperature is $\hbar c^3/8\pi GMk_B$, as without the string, so its entropy is lower than that of a black hole of the same temperature without one [achucarro1995].¶Aryal, Ford, and Vilenkin also discussed a pair of black holes held apart by strings [aryal1986]. That solution is nearly identical to a static, axially symmetric solution that Rudolf Bach and Hermann Weyl gave in 1922 [aryal1986, bach1922]. They showed how such solutions, "formerly a mathematical curiosity", "may be given a more physical interpretation in terms of cosmic strings" [aryal1986]. A single string that ends on a black hole accelerates it uniformly, and that spacetime is the C-metric, whose conical singularity William Kinnersley and Martin Walker identified in 1970 as the force on the accelerating mass [kinnersley1970, achucarro1995]. Gregory and Mark Hindmarsh constructed in 1995 two metrics for vortices ending on black holes, in which the fields of the vortex smooth out the conical singularities [gregory1995].¶A cosmic string in a gauge theory is a vortex with a core, the Nielsen-Olesen vortex of the Abelian Higgs model, and the null geodesics that generate a static horizon must stay free of convergence and shear where they cross that core [achucarro1995]. Fay Dowker, Gregory, and Jennie Traschen found in 1992 a vortex sitting at the horizon of the Euclidean Schwarzschild solution, whose back reaction cuts a slice out of that geometry [dowker1992]. Achúcarro, Gregory, and Kuijken showed, with an analytic approximation for strings thin compared with the black hole and with numerical solutions, that a Nielsen-Olesen vortex threads the horizon of a Schwarzschild black hole, and with its back reaction they recovered the metric of Aryal, Ford, and Vilenkin [achucarro1995]. They defined hair as "a charge or property of the black hole measurable at infinity" and concluded that the vortex is hair, since the deficit angle is measurable there [achucarro1995]. Filipe Bonjour, Roberto Emparan, and Gregory proved in 1999 that an extreme charged black hole expels the flux of a vortex in some cases and is pierced by it in others, and gave a bound for each [bonjour1999]. With David Kubizňák and Danielle Wills, Gregory put the vortex through a Kerr black hole in 2013 and found its back reaction conical with respect to a local frame rotating with the hole [gregory2013].¶Steven Lonsdale and Ian Moss calculated in 1988 the cross section for a black hole to capture a moving string [lonsdale1988]. Dmitri Gal'tsov and E. Masar described the geodesics of the conical Schwarzschild spacetime in detail in 1989 [galtsov1989]. Jean-Pierre De Villiers and Valeri Frolov solved numerically, in 1998, the motion of a straight string that approaches a Schwarzschild black hole from a great distance, and obtained the impact parameter for capture as a function of the string's velocity [devilliers1998]. Achúcarro, Gregory, and Kuijken argued that a merger conserves the internal energy of the black hole, so that its gravitational mass grows by $4GM\mu/c^2 = 2r_s\mu$, the mass of the length of string it swallows [achucarro1995]. Michael Appels, Gregory, and Kubizňák let the tension vary in 2017 and added to the first law of this black hole the term $-2\lambda\,\delta\mu$, with a thermodynamic length $\lambda$ conjugate to the tension at each pole [appels2017]. Vilenkin, Yuri Levin, and Andrei Gruzinov showed in 2018 that primordial black holes forming in a universe that holds cosmic strings capture about ten long strings each, and that the holes and strings form networks [vilenkin2018].

related.text: The black hole with the string pulled out, $b = 1$, where the missing wedge closes.
The string with the black hole taken out, $r_s = 0$, which leaves a flat cone.
A black hole with a string on one side alone. That string pulls it into uniform acceleration [kinnersley1970, achucarro1995].
The rotating black hole. A string through it leaves a cone as well, measured in a frame that turns with the hole, as Ruth Gregory, David Kubizňák, and Danielle Wills found in 2013 [gregory2013].

coordinates.name: Static

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, with $M$ the gravitational mass
$b = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$, with $\mu$ the string's mass per unit length, equal to its tension, $0 < b \le 1$; the deficit angle is $2\pi(1 - b)$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\phi$ periodic in $2\pi$, the deficit carried by $g_{\phi\phi} = b^2r^2\sin^2\theta$.

coordinates.name: Static with the Wedge Removed

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, with $M$ the gravitational mass
$b = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$, with $\mu$ the string's mass per unit length, equal to its tension, $0 < b \le 1$; the deficit angle is $2\pi(1 - b)$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \tilde\phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\tilde\phi = b\phi$ periodic in $2\pi b$, so that the line element is Schwarzschild's.

coordinates.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, with $M$ the gravitational mass
$b = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$, with $\mu$ the string's mass per unit length, equal to its tension, $0 < b \le 1$; the deficit angle is $2\pi(1 - b)$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the retarded time $u = ct - r - r_s\ln\left|r/r_s - 1\right|$ a length and $\phi$ periodic in $2\pi$.

coordinates.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, with $M$ the gravitational mass
$b = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$, with $\mu$ the string's mass per unit length, equal to its tension, $0 < b \le 1$; the deficit angle is $2\pi(1 - b)$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the advanced time $v = ct + r + r_s\ln\left|r/r_s - 1\right|$ a length and $\phi$ periodic in $2\pi$.
